items.title: Long-Context Drafting Does Not Require Long-Context Drafters
items.headline: Frozen short-context speculative drafters keep their speedup out to 2M tokens using a capped drafter KV cache and RoPE index remapping
items.summary: At very long context a speculative-decoding drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so its speedup shrinks and can turn into a slowdown; the usual fix is training a long-context drafter or relying on an MTP head. The authors argue current drafters already read the target's hidden states over the whole prefix, so they do not need their own long attention. They keep released short-context drafters frozen and add two inference-time changes: (1) cap the attention cache the drafter sees, fixing its per-token cost, and (2) remap rotary position indices back into the drafter's trained range. No weights change; one tunable parameter, which the paper says plateaus early. They also prove when a constant index shift leaves the drafter's computation unchanged and decompose acceptance into two measurable gaps with bounds.
items.result: Per the abstract, one vLLM configuration works from 4k to 2M tokens; the frozen drafter's short-context speedup is retained out to 2M tokens across 3 target–drafter pairs and 5 corpora, at a cost of at most 0.16x speedup at short lengths. Ablating either mechanism removes the flat speedup curve. The abstract gives no absolute speedup numbers.
items.critique: The claim is explicitly about the speedup staying flat, not about its size, so it says nothing about how fast this is versus trained long-context drafters or MTP heads; whether those baselines were compared head-to-head is not stated in the abstract. Only three target–drafter pairs. The authors note the benefit holds only while speculative cost per emitted token stays below target-only decoding. No code link on the arXiv page. Read from the abstract only; the HTML version was rate-limited.

items.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
items.headline: RoLaQ quantizes MLA's shared latent KV cache to 2 bits; SGLang build on DeepSeek-V2-Lite reports 3.96x KV capacity, 2.51x decode at 256K
items.summary: In multi-head latent attention (DeepSeek-style MLA), each token's KV is a single shared latent, so at 2 bits the quantization error hits both key matching and value readout, and how much depends on the error's direction and the reconstruction scale. RoLaQ is an offline calibration that jointly learns (a) a shared rotation, refined only within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value up-projections, and (b) coupled range thresholds and reconstruction gains for the latent. Calibration uses prediction matching plus attention-output supervision; model weights stay frozen.
items.result: Across 3 MLA models and 6 benchmarks, RoLaQ has the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods, both with and without token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation holds 3.96x the BF16 KV capacity in the same memory budget and gives 2.51x decode throughput at 256K input tokens.
items.critique: The abstract does not name the 2-bit baselines or give accuracy deltas versus BF16, so how much quality is lost at 2 bits is unknown from what was read. The systems numbers are on DeepSeek-V2-Lite (a small MLA model), not a frontier-scale MLA model. 'Token protection' (keeping some tokens at higher precision) changes the effective bit budget; how many tokens are kept is not stated. No code link on the arXiv page.

items.title: SpectrumQuant: Spectrum Alignment for LLM Quantization
items.headline: SpectrumQuant builds closed-form, covariance-aware rotations for LLM PTQ; competitive with learned rotations using under 1/3 the GPU memory
items.summary: Rotation-based PTQ (QuaRot/SpinQuant style) applies orthogonal transforms that preserve the function but reshape activations for low-bit quantization; existing choices are fixed Hadamard rotations or rotations learned during calibration. The authors derive, from first principles, that maximizing covariance yields spectral alignment, and build a closed-form transform from activation covariance estimated on calibration data. The rotation is framed as an alignment component plus a mixing component; Hadamard matrices are a special case and a class of butterfly matrices fits the same framework.
items.result: On Llama and Mistral models, SpectrumQuant is reported competitive with leading rotation strategies while using less than one-third of the GPU memory and running significantly faster than the learned-rotation methods SpinQuant and DartQuant.
items.critique: 'Competitive' is not quantified in the abstract (no bit-widths, perplexity or accuracy deltas), and the speed advantage is stated without numbers. Model sizes and versions are not given. A data-dependent covariance estimate may be sensitive to calibration-set choice; whether that was ablated is not stated. No code link on the arXiv page.

items.title: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training
items.headline: LCT Huffman-codes weights, activations and optimizer states on GPU in training: 24.6% less memory on a 162M NanoGPT for 7.2% slower steps
items.summary: Lossless compression could cut training memory, but training re-encodes tensors every step, so encode/decode overhead dominates. LCT is a GPU framework built for that repeated cycle: it exploits redundancy in floating-point data (e.g. exponent bits) to compress weights, activations and optimizer states, using custom GPU Huffman kernels with precomputed codebooks to keep overhead low. The paper also analyzes storage cost and how the scheme copes with shifts in tensor magnitude over training.
items.result: Compression ratios up to 1.455x. On a 162M-parameter NanoGPT, 24.6% lower memory use for a 7.2% increase in step time. In Qwen3-4B fine-tuning, up to 23.8% lower peak memory, allowing 3.5x longer training context on the same GPU.
items.critique: Small scale: a 162M pretraining run and a 4B fine-tune; behaviour in multi-GPU sharded training (FSDP/ZeRO, where memory is already partitioned) is not described in the abstract. No comparison is stated against standard memory savers such as activation checkpointing, 8-bit optimizer states or CPU offload, which trade compute for memory in a similar way. The 1.455x ratio is an upper bound ('up to'). No code link on the arXiv page.

items.title: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation
items.headline: Merges same-base specialists into one model by solving per-layer least squares from forward-pass second moments, with no gradient steps
items.summary: On-policy distillation of several specialists into one student normally needs rollouts, teacher passes and gradient updates per teacher. When all specialists share a base model, the authors show distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer must reproduce each specialist's outputs on the inputs that specialist sees while generating its own answers, which is a least-squares problem needing only the input second moments. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts per specialist provides those statistics. They also find rollout content matters more than the solver: answers stuck in repetition loops are rare but take a large share of a math specialist's tokens, and filtering them out is key.
items.result: Removing looped rollouts raises the fused model's AIME25 score from task-arithmetic level to the specialist's level at matched precision. On Olmo 3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist give a generalist that keeps most of each specialist's gains across 7 math and code benchmarks; the abstract says the fused model is on average more accurate than any single specialist.
items.critique: Only one 7B base model and only math/code specialists. 'Keeps most of the gains' is not quantified in the abstract, and comparisons to stronger merging baselines (TIES, DARE, or actual gradient-based on-policy distillation) are not stated beyond task arithmetic. Requires a shared base model. The layer-wise solve treats layers independently, so error compounding across depth is a natural concern not addressed in the abstract. No code link on the arXiv page.

items.title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
items.headline: Edge0 streams a 35B MoE from SSD at 20 tok/s with 3 GiB peak active memory, using a trained head that predicts next-layer routing
items.summary: A 35B-class MoE needs about 19.5 GB at 4-bit; sparsity cuts compute per token but not bytes stored, and naive SSD offload fails because layer N+1's experts are only known after layer N runs, so reads cannot overlap compute. Edge0 adds a per-layer 'prerouter' head that predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, and then uses that prediction as the actual routing, so prefetched experts always match the experts used. An unmerged recovery LoRA, trained on this student path, recovers quality lost to int4 quantization and the routing replacement. Framework, checkpoints and adapters are released (github.com/Edge0-AI/edge0, per the HF page).
items.result: On a single 24 GB machine, a 35B MoE runs at 20 tok/s with 3 GiB peak active memory, staying within a few points of its fp16 teacher averaged over 5 public benchmarks. An 8B tier runs on the same framework.
items.critique: Not a new paper (submitted 16–17 Sep 2026); included because it is currently trending on Hugging Face and was not covered before. Replacing the router with a predicted router changes the model, so this is a modified model rather than lossless offloading; 'within a few points' is not quantified on the HF page. Throughput depends heavily on SSD bandwidth, and the hardware is described only as a 24 GB machine. Comparison against existing offload engines is not stated in the abstract.

items.title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
items.headline: FPoT uses a base-√2 weight grid for 4-bit, multiplier-free shift-add LLM inference, closing most of the gap to uniform INT4
items.summary: Power-of-two (PoT) weight quantization lets matmuls run with shifts and adds instead of multipliers, but its grid is too coarse at 4 bits. FPoT uses a half-octave grid (base √2) so 4-bit weights get finer resolution while the datapath stays fully integer shift-add. It is designed to compose with existing LLM PTQ methods.
items.result: On Llama-3-8B at 4-bit weights and activations, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense-reasoning accuracy by 8.72% over the PoT baseline and stays close to the uniform-integer baseline. Reported to hold across 7 models and 3 bit-widths.
items.critique: The benefit is hardware efficiency, but the abstract reports accuracy only; no area, energy or latency measurements on real or simulated multiplier-free hardware are stated. Whether 8.72% is absolute points or relative is not clear from the abstract. Commonsense zero-shot tasks are a soft benchmark for 4-bit degradation; perplexity and harder reasoning tasks are not mentioned. Representing √2 multiples with shift-add needs extra adds, whose cost is not quantified in the abstract. No code link on the arXiv page.

items.title: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
items.headline: LangDiT, a transformer backbone built for continuous diffusion LMs, gets 21.72 GenPPL at 1024 NFEs on OpenWebText as a LangFlow drop-in
items.summary: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) usually borrow backbones from autoregressive LLMs or image Diffusion Transformers. The authors study the architecture space for CDLMs and propose the Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT): feature and QK normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing with calibration, and confidence-gated self-conditioning during training. Representation, training objective and sampler are held fixed, so the gains are attributed to the backbone.
items.result: As a drop-in backbone for LangFlow, unconditional generation of 1024-token OpenWebText sequences reaches GenPPL 21.72 at 1024 NFEs and 44.72 at 128 NFEs; under Plaid-style formulations, 11.33 at 1024 NFEs and 27.51 at 128. The abstract says it substantially lowers GenPPL versus matched LangFlow baselines, but the baseline numbers are not given in what was read.
items.critique: Generative perplexity alone can be gamed by low-diversity samples; no entropy/diversity numbers are given in the abstract. Model size and training compute are not stated. No downstream or conditional tasks. Several changes are bundled together; per-component ablations are not described in the abstract. Read via a deeplearn.org mirror of the arXiv abstract (arXiv:2610.22330) because arXiv was rate-limiting this run.

items.title: Close Enough is Nowhere Near: Fidelity-Consumability Decoupling in KV Caches
items.headline: Swapping one frozen LLM's KV cache in for another's fails across 8 substitution methods; attending over it as extra context works instead
items.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems could pass KV caches instead of text to avoid recomputation. The authors test the simplest case: both models frozen and the sender's cache directly replaces the reader's, with no training. They argue a frozen reader can only use caches inside a narrow 'tolerable set' near its own, that geometric similarity to its own cache does not predict usability, and that performance falls off abruptly (attributed to competitive attention), so making substitutes more faithful does not help. The alternative they test: the reader keeps its own cache and attends over the sender's as extra context, adapting only its queries.
items.result: All 8 substitution methods land at the uninformative-cache baseline rather than at the reader's own read-the-passage accuracy. The keep-own-cache design with query adaptation beats the reader's baseline, and with 8 senders pooled still clears it, while undirected attention over the same pooled cache falls below it.
items.critique: The authors frame it as a characterization on a single probe task, not a benchmark result; models, sizes and absolute accuracies are not given in the abstract. The positive design needs query adaptation (some training), so it is not a training-free fix. Relevance to single-model inference efficiency is indirect, hence off focus. No code link on the arXiv page.
